By the end of this week you can:

Build frequency and relative-frequency tables and choose an honest bar chart over a misleading
one.
Read a two-way (contingency) table; compute row/column (conditional) proportions.
Judge whether two categorical variables appear associated from a segmented bar chart.
State probability as long-run relative frequency and give the sample space of a simple process.

Every fall, the SPCA-style shelter near campus takes in a few hundred cats and dogs and tracks two
simple facts about each one: how big it is, and whether it gets adopted. Down the street, a coffee
shop tracks a different pair of facts: what time of day a customer orders, and what they order. Both
places are sitting on

— labels, not numbers — and both questions (“does size
matter for adoption?” “does the order change by time of day?”) are questions about whether two
categories move together. This week you’ll learn to organize that kind of data honestly, read it out
of a table, and take your first step into

: using what already happened to say something
about what’s likely to happen next.

children.label: Counting categories: frequency tables and honest bar charts

as a proportion (a decimal between 0 and 1) or a percent (the proportion × 100).

A bar chart’s y-axis should always
start at 0; if it doesn’t, treat every visual comparison with suspicion.

: humans are bad at comparing the areas of wedges (especially more than 3–4 of them, or
any wedge drawn in fake “3-D” that distorts the front slices), so a table or bar chart is almost always
the more honest and more readable choice.

Those three conditional numbers — 77.5%, 62.7%, 37.3% — tell a clear story: the adoption rate drops
steadily as size goes up. That pattern is exactly what a

is built to show. In a segmented bar for each size category, the “Adopted” portion
shrinks from about three-quarters of the Small bar, to about two-thirds of the Medium bar, to just
over a third of the Large bar. Because the

proportions change noticeably across size
categories, size and adoption outcome appear

— if they weren’t, all three bars would
show roughly the same 60% adopted / 40% not-adopted split as the marginal total.

children.alt: A stacked (segmented) bar chart with one bar per size category, each bar's height filling 100%. Within each bar, the Adopted segment shrinks from about 77.5% of the Small bar, to 62.7% of the Medium bar, to 37.3% of the Large bar -- a visibly decreasing share that signals size and adoption outcome are associated, not independent.

There’s no dedicated “two-way table” menu on the TI-83/84 — you build the table by hand and compute
each proportion with plain arithmetic. Enter one size category’s counts into a list (

= Not-adopted counts) so you can add across a column for a total.
To turn any count into a clean fraction or decimal, type

to see it as a fraction, or leave it as a decimal and read the percent by moving the decimal point two
places (e.g.,

library(mosaic)

# colorblind-safe (Okabe-Ito) fills, never rely on hue alone --
# the segment/bar labels below also state each percentage in words
ok_2 <- c("#0072B2", "#E69F00")            # Adopted / Not adopted
ok_3 <- c("#0072B2", "#E69F00", "#009E73") # Drip / Latte / ColdBrew

# frequency & relative-frequency table (Example 1)
tally(~ size, data = shelter_sim)
tally(~ size, data = shelter_sim, format = "percent")

# two-way table and conditional proportions: P(adopted | size)
tally(adopted ~ size, data = shelter_sim, margins = TRUE)
tally(adopted ~ size, data = shelter_sim, format = "proportion")

# segmented bar chart (Figure 2)
gf_props(~ size, data = shelter_sim, fill = ~ adopted, position = "fill") %>%
  gf_refine(scale_fill_manual(values = ok_2))

# empirical probability from a marginal table (Example 2)
tally(~ order, data = coffee_sim, format = "proportion")
gf_bar(~ order, data = coffee_sim, fill = ~ order) %>%
  gf_refine(scale_fill_manual(values = ok_3))

# long-run relative frequency demo (Figure 3)
do(1000) * rflip(1)

Durable skill: quantitative communication & critical thinking

Cross-tabulated data — sales by region, satisfaction by department, defects by shift — shows up in
almost every workplace slide deck. Knowing how to pull the

proportion out of a two-way table
(marginal vs. conditional), and knowing to distrust a bar chart whose axis doesn’t start at 0, are
skills you’ll use to build honest reports and catch misleading ones long after this course ends.
